summary: Convincing Industrial Age direction with four distinguishable everyday roles. The Alderman is the strongest design: tall hat, dark formal coat and oversized civic collar communicate authority immediately. Revise the mechanic’s cap, the clerk’s skirt construction and the caravan leader’s distant-origin identity.
problems: The mechanic’s cap reads as a large rectangular slab in both variants, not a low, sloping flat cap. The empty tray provides little occupational identification.
The clerk’s skirt reads as two trouser-like box shells, particularly on the taller character. The central split and straight panel edges undermine the bustle-dress silhouette.
The messenger and railway baron have broad, rigid shoulder blocks that read more like shoulder armour than draped pelerines.
The railway baron reads as a well-dressed local traveller. The tiny luggage markings cannot establish distant origin or railway affiliation at stream scale.
Much of the secondary identification depends on tiny buttons, chains and labels; these should support, not substitute for, larger silhouette and colour cues.
fix: Workshop Mechanic: Rebuild the cap with a shallow, tapered crown flowing into a short peak; eliminate the large square outline visible in this render and seat it closely against the head. Add one chunky hammer or spanner projecting above the tray rim, with the handle clearly held. Municipal Clerk: Replace the parallel box-shell appearance with slightly flared, layered skirt panels. Stagger front and rear edges so the centre reads as a fabric opening rather than a trouser division; retain separate leg attachment and test clearance through walking poses. Preserve the puff sleeves, bustle, bun and ledger. Market Provisioner: Keep the broad hat, cream bib and colourful hamper; these already distinguish the role. Refine the lower apron panels into thinner, slightly overlapping-looking canvas flaps at rest, without joining the legs, and preserve a visible hand-to-handle grip. Telegraph Messenger: Keep the peaked cap, diagonal satchel and contrasting stockings. Thin the shoulder pieces, slope their outer edges downward and align them visually with the rear cape so they read as cloth rather than rigid pads. Alderman: Retain the tall top hat, dark coat and large medallion. Seat the collar links close to the garment and continue the gold treatment over the shoulders for stronger overhead recognition; no major redesign needed. Railway Baron: Preserve the cream coat and bowler contrast with the Alderman, but soften the shoulder slabs into a draped, articulated cape. Introduce a bold invented distant-railway identity: a broad contrasting cape border and matching large locomotive or winged-wheel crest on the luggage. Move the luggage marking onto its outward-facing side and enlarge it substantially; keep all handles and carried documents visibly seated in the hands.
